name: fdisk
description: The classic interactive partition table tool for MBR and GPT disks.

flags.description: List partition tables of all (or the given) disks.
Enter interactive mode. Inside: n new, d delete, t change type, p print, w write, q quit without saving.

examples.output:
Disk /dev/sda: 238.5 GiB, 256060514304 bytes
Device     Boot  Start    End Sectors  Size Id Type
/dev/sda1  *      2048 1050623 1048576  512M ef EFI
/dev/sda2       1050624 ...        238G 83 Linux
examples.explanation: Lists every disk with its partition layout. The Id/Type column shows EFI, Linux, swap, etc.
Interactive partitioning of /dev/sdb: press n (new partition), accept defaults, t (type 8e for LVM or 20 for Linux), w (write). NOTHING is changed until w.

about: fdisk edits the partition table in memory and writes it on w. GPT is the modern standard (UEFI boot, disks > 2 TB); MBR survives for legacy BIOS. parted and sfdisk offer non-interactive alternatives; gdisk is fdisk's dedicated GPT cousin. After changes, run partprobe or partx -u so the kernel re-reads the table.
useCases: Create partitions for LVM or filesystems.
mistakes: Forgetting w in interactive mode and losing all your work.
Operating on the wrong disk — triple-check the device name (lsblk first!).
warnings: fdisk writes directly to the disk. A wrong target destroys data. Always confirm with lsblk which disk is which before starting.
distroNotes: util-linux fdisk supports GPT fully on all modern distributions. DOS-fdisk-era limitations no longer apply.
